title: Some antique glassware contains uranium, and it glows bright green under UV light

cover.alt: A moulded glass vase with a chevron pattern glowing vivid green against a black background under ultraviolet light.

body: Glassmakers once added uranium, usually as a diuranate compound, to the glass mix before melting it, to tint the glass yellow to green. The amount usually ranges from trace levels to **about 2% uranium by weight**. Under an ultraviolet lamp, the uranium makes the glass glow a bright, eerie green. A sensitive Geiger counter can pick up its radiation above the background, but most pieces are considered harmless and only negligibly radioactive.

left.label: Daylight
left.text: Pale yellow to green glass, with nothing unusual about it.

right.label: Ultraviolet
right.text: A vivid green glow, given off by the uranium in the glass.

slides.heading: Up to about 2% of a typical piece, by weight, is uranium
slides.note: Usually trace levels to about 2%; some 20th-century pieces reportedly held up to 25%

slides.clue: The word for absorbing ultraviolet light and giving off a visible glow, as uranium glass does
slides.detail: Uranium glass fluoresces bright green under ultraviolet light, even when it looks only pale yellow-green in daylight.

events.text: Reported in a Roman mosaic near Naples
Franz Xaver Riedel blows it in Bohemia
US uranium goes to the Manhattan Project

slides.alt: A glass vacuum capacitor with metal end caps, joined to the glass by small pale green rings of uranium glass.
slides.caption: The pale green rings on this vacuum capacitor are uranium glass. Glassblowers use it as a go-between when sealing metals such as tungsten into glass.

slides.question: In the 1930s, pale yellow-green uranium glass got a nickname. What was it?
slides.explanation: Its colour looked like the petroleum jelly of the day. US production stopped in the middle of World War II, when uranium was taken for the Manhattan Project.
